paragraphs.text: A guided reading journey with Try Jesus Media
313 readings with simple guidance, questions, and room for notes
Bring your Bible. Follow the story. Take one small step at a time.

Copyright © 2026 Try Jesus Media. The guidance and arrangement in this edition were created for this reading journey. This book includes Bible references, not the full text of a Bible translation. No rights are claimed in Bible references.

References were checked against the repository's 66-book KJV data at assets/bible/kjv.json, identified there as the eBible.org ENG-KJV2006 edition. The explanations in this guide are our own. They are not part of the Bible text.
Welcome. Bring a Bible translation you enjoy reading. This guide will help you follow the story, ask questions, and find a next step. There is room for your notes, too.
You'll follow 313 readings through 11 sections. Take your time. Notice what the passage says, ask honest questions, and think about how it speaks to your life. There is no race to finish.

The plan covers all 1,189 chapters of this 66-book Bible, with each verse assigned once. Follow the passage shown beside each checkbox. Some chapters are split between readings or into smaller parts within a reading.
Some passages may leave you puzzled or sad. It's okay to pause. Read a little more around the passage, or talk with someone you trust. You don't need every answer to take the next step.

Ask God for guidance God promises that if you seek Him, you will find Him (Jeremiah 29:13). As you pray and read your Bible, you will get to know your Creator and Redeemer.
Read the Bible Read the assigned passage. Notice whether you are reading a story, poem, law, prophecy, Gospel, letter, or vision.
Find your place The short introduction helps you see where this reading fits. Some accounts overlap, and some dates are uncertain.
Notice one thing: Use the prompt to look more closely. What does the passage say? What are you still wondering about?
Talk or reflect Try the question on your own or with others. Share only what you feel comfortable sharing. Listening is welcome, too.
Try a small step Each suggestion is an invitation. Choose what fits your situation. Give yourself time if you need more understanding, support, or advice.
Make a note Write something you noticed, a question, or a next step. A few words are enough. You can come back to it later.
Check your progress Tick each box when you've read its assigned verses. Then tick Reading complete. If a chapter appears again, follow the verses listed there.
Getting to know God through Bible reading is not a race or a competition. It is a time of reflection, self-revelation, and relationship. This takes time and is meant to be enjoyed.
Been away for a while? Find your last reading, glance at its introduction, and take the next small step.

Lost your place in the story? Read the section introduction. Feeling tired? Read a smaller part and check it off when you're done. If a passage is upsetting, pause and seek support. You can go slowly.
You might pray: “Father, help me listen, understand, and take the next step with You.”

Stories tell what happened; they don't approve of everything people did. Poems use pictures, repetition, and feeling. Wisdom sayings describe patterns in life. Read them together, not as promises that life will always go one way.

Laws first guided ancient Israel's life with God. Prophets spoke to real people with warnings and hope. Letters need to be read as a whole. Visions use symbols and earlier Bible images; they offer more than a timetable.
Name the passage and give everyone time to find it. Invite each person to share one thing they noticed. Then try the question. Let it start a conversation.
Finish with one thing to remember and, if you wish, one small step. No one has to share private feelings, agree, or make a promise. Listening counts.
For Try Jesus Media's current community and discussion options, visit https://tryjesusmedia.com/welcome.
Online groups and resources may change. Check the member page for current details.
Here is the path through the book. It shows the order of the sections, not how many years each one covers. Some books and visions overlap in time.
01  The Beginning Creation, the early world, and Job
02  Abraham and Family Abraham's family and the move to Egypt
03  Moses and Israel Deliverance from Egypt and the wilderness journey
04  Israel Before It Had Kings Settlement in Canaan and the period of the judges
05  Israel With Kings Samuel, Saul, David, and Solomon
06  The Divided Kingdom The early northern and southern kingdoms
07  Assyria and the Exile Years Assyria's conquest, Judah's crisis, and the exile years
08  Babylon's Fall and the First Return Belshazzar, Babylon's fall, and the beginning of return
09  Rebuilding and Restoration Temple work and Jewish community life under Persia
10  Jesus and the Fulfillment of the Old Testament The birth, ministry, death, and resurrection of Jesus
11  The Disciples Spread the Gospel The early church and the hope of new creation
The divided kingdom at a glance
Kings and Chronicles move between two kingdoms. Use this guide to keep track. Sometimes Israel means all God's people, not just the northern kingdom.
Ask which northern king is named
Ask which king rules in Jerusalem

Egypt is southwest of Israel and Judah. Assyria and Babylon are to the east and northeast, in Mesopotamia. Later, Persia rules as people return home. In the New Testament, the good news spreads around the eastern Mediterranean toward Greece and Rome. These are ancient places, not a guide to today's borders.

These 313 readings follow the story as closely as the Bible's dates allow. Related accounts in Kings, Chronicles, and the Gospels appear together. Some chapters are split into smaller passages. Follow the references and checkboxes in each reading.

Some passages look back or cover many years. Family lists, summaries of a king's reign, and poems do not date every detail. A prophet may speak about the future. Some dates and the order of related events remain uncertain.

Job appears before Abraham in this plan, but we do not know when he lived. Dates for Joel, Obadiah, many psalms, and several letters are also uncertain. Psalms that name an event appear near it; that does not tell us when the poem was written. Notes explain other date questions where they affect the order.

After the kingdom divides, keep northern Israel and southern Judah in view. Judah and Benjamin are the main southern tribes, with Levites and others also present; see 1 Kings 12 and 2 Chronicles 11:13-17. The story then follows Assyria, Judah's fall, exile, Babylon's fall, and the return to rebuild.

This is a Christian guide. Where the New Testament connects a passage to Jesus, we show that link. Broader links are labeled as themes. Read the Bible passages for yourself, and remember that this guide's explanations are not the Bible text.
You are here Creation, the early world, and Job
Before this Beginning of the plan
Where we are Genesis begins with creation. It shows people receiving God's gifts, breaking trust, and hurting one another.
The big question How can people live well when trust is broken? Job asks another hard question: why do people suffer when they have done nothing wrong?
People Adam and Eve; Cain and Abel; Noah; Job and his friends
Places Eden; the world of the flood; Babel; the land of Uz
A little help as you begin

Begin with God's gifts and his care for people, even after they fail. Notice relationships with God, each other, and the world. Genesis 1-11 leads toward Abraham's call. Job comes next in this plan, but we do not know when he lived.

Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. John 1:1-5 uses creation language to introduce the Word. Romans 5:12-21 compares Adam and Christ. Read Genesis first, then explore those connections.
As you read: God's gifts, people's choices, broken trust, and continuing mercy.
Pause here After Reading 009, think about the value God gives people and the limits we all share.
What would you like to understand as you begin?
Creation, the Fall, and the Promise
In this reading God creates a good world. People break trust, yet God continues to care for them.
As you read: Notice God's blessing, the people's hiding, and how God reaches out.
Talk or reflect What does this passage show about our value and our choices?
Try this Notice one way God cares for people after they fail.

Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. Romans 5:12-21 contrasts Adam and Christ; John 1:1-5 returns to creation language. Read those passages after reading Genesis in its own setting.
Cain, Seth, and the Generations Before Noah
In this reading Life continues outside Eden. Violence grows, but people also begin calling on the Lord.
As you read: Compare Cain's response to correction with the growing reach of violence.
Talk or reflect What helps resentment grow, and what might help it soften?
Try this Try one small act that makes room for peace.
In this reading The flood brings judgment on a violent world. God's promise gives Noah's family a new beginning.
As you read: Follow God's concern for life before and after the flood.
Talk or reflect What comes with the gift of a fresh start?
Try this Thank God for a new beginning and consider how to care for it.

Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. First Peter 3:18-22 draws on Noah's story in a difficult passage about salvation and baptism. Follow Peter's argument without giving every detail a hidden meaning.
The Nations and the Tower of Babel
In this reading Noah's descendants become nations. At Babel, people seek greatness and safety on their own terms.
As you read: Compare the people's wish for a great name with God's scattering them.
Talk or reflect What were the people at Babel hoping to gain?
Try this Think about what helps a community belong without needing to impress.
Job's Trials and the First Speeches
In this reading Before Abraham's story, we meet Job. He suffers deeply, and his friends struggle to understand why.
As you read: Separate what the narrator tells us from what Job's friends assume.
Talk or reflect What helps a hurting person feel heard?
Try this Listen to someone without trying to explain their pain.

Connection to Jesus A shared Christian theme. James 5:11 recalls Job's endurance and the Lord's compassion. Jesus' invitation to the weary in Matthew 11:28-30 also offers a basis for patient hope. Neither passage promises every sufferer Job's particular restoration.
Job and His Friends Continue the Debate
In this reading Job's friends blame him for his suffering. Their answers do not fit what he has lived through.
As you read: Hear both Job's longing for God and his frustration with his friends.
Talk or reflect What do Job's friends assume about suffering?
Try this Bring an honest question to God.
In this reading Job's pain continues. He asks hard questions while reaching for justice and hope.
As you read: Notice that hope and protest can appear in the same speech.
Talk or reflect How can a prayer hold both sadness and hope?
Try this Write a few words of honest prayer.
Job's Final Defense and Elihu Begins
In this reading Job remembers his earlier life and defends his honesty. Elihu joins the conversation with more answers about suffering.
As you read: Compare confident claims about God with the limits of each speaker's knowledge.
Talk or reflect What makes it easier to listen when we don't understand?
Try this Leave room to say, I don't know.
Elihu, God's Answer, and Job's Restoration
In this reading God answers Job with questions about creation. Job sees the limits of his understanding, and God corrects his friends.
As you read: Notice what God says about the friends, not just how religious their words sound.
Talk or reflect Can trust grow while questions remain?
Try this Ask God for humility and care for others.

Connection to Jesus A shared Christian theme. Job's encounter with divine wisdom invites reflection on human limits. Colossians 2:3 locates the treasures of wisdom and knowledge in Christ. This is a thematic comparison, not an identification of Job's speeches as direct predictions of Jesus.
What has Job helped you see about suffering? What would you like to explore further?
Next, the story turns to one family. Through them, God promises to bless others.
Ready to continue? Begin with the next section. Go at your own pace.
You are here Abraham's family and the move to Egypt
Where we are The nations have grown apart. God calls Abraham and promises a blessing that will reach others.
The big question Will this family trust God while they wait? Jealousy, lies, hunger, and years of waiting test them.
People Abraham and Sarah; Isaac and Rebekah; Jacob and Esau; Joseph and his brothers
Places Canaan; Haran and the wider Mesopotamian setting; Egypt
A little help as you begin

Follow God's promises of family, land, and blessing. The people who receive them have faith, but they also make painful choices. Notice those with less power. Joseph's suffering becomes part of his family's survival. By the end, they are safe in Egypt, still waiting for their promised home.

Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. Galatians 3:8, 16 connects God's promise to Abraham with the good news and Christ. Matthew 1:1 introduces Jesus as a descendant of Abraham and David.
As you read: Who receives a promise? How do their choices affect others?
Pause here After Reading 017, find one way someone in the family has changed.
What would you like to understand as you begin?
In this reading God calls Abraham and promises to bless others through his family. Trust will grow through waiting and difficulty.
As you read: Follow God's promise through waiting, trust, and attempts to take control.
Talk or reflect How might a blessing reach beyond the person receiving it?
Try this Share something good with someone outside your usual circle.
Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. Galatians 3:8, 16 connects the promise to Abraham with the gospel and Christ. Notice that blessing is meant to reach the nations.
In this reading God's promise moves toward Isaac's birth. Abraham's family meets guests, danger, hard choices, and unexpected help.
As you read: Notice where God's provision exceeds Abraham's ability to secure the future.
Talk or reflect Where does Abraham receive help he cannot provide himself?
Try this Bring something precious to God in prayer.

Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. Hebrews 11:17-19 interprets Abraham's test through trust in God's power to raise the dead. Begin there before developing broader comparisons with Jesus' sacrifice.
Genesis 24; Genesis 25:1-6; Genesis 25:12-16; Genesis 25:19-26; Genesis 25:7-11; Genesis 25:27-34; Genesis 26; Genesis 25:17-18
In this reading Abraham and Sarah's generation passes. Isaac's family carries the promise forward through marriage, inheritance, and conflict.
As you read: The ages place Jacob and Esau's birth before Abraham's death. Family summaries and the Gerar story do not date every event.
Talk or reflect What good things can one generation pass to the next?
Try this Give thanks for one good thing you've received.
In this reading Jacob deceives his family and leaves home. Away from home, he meets both God's promise and painful family conflict.
As you read: Watch how Jacob encounters the kinds of manipulation he practiced.
Talk or reflect How do lies affect trust in this family?
Try this Choose a small, honest step in a relationship.
In this reading Jacob returns to Esau and faces fear, peace, loss, and family trouble. Isaac's death appears later, during Joseph's time in Egypt.
As you read: Genesis 35:28-29 appears in Reading 015: the ages place Isaac's death after Joseph was sold. Family lists give background, not dates for each person.
Talk or reflect What helps peace grow without ignoring hurt or boundaries?
Try this Consider a safe, thoughtful step toward honesty or peace.
In this reading Joseph is sold into Egypt and later imprisoned. After Isaac's death, Joseph rises to serve under Pharaoh.
As you read: Read Genesis 35:28-29 between chapters 40 and 41. The age clues are in Genesis 25:26; 37:2; 41:46; 45:6; and 47:9.
Talk or reflect How does Joseph serve in a situation he didn't choose?
Try this Notice one responsibility you can care for today.

Connection to Jesus A shared Christian theme. Joseph's undeserved suffering and later care for others can be compared with Jesus' self-giving service in Philippians 2:5-8. Acts 7 retells Joseph's story without identifying every event as a prediction of Jesus.
In this reading Famine brings Joseph's brothers to Egypt. Old guilt surfaces, and their choices begin to show change.
As you read: Look for changed behavior, especially when another brother becomes vulnerable.
Talk or reflect How do the brothers show they have changed?
Try this Try one action that shows a change of heart.
Israel in Egypt and Jacob's Final Blessings
In this reading Jacob's family settles in Egypt. Even as loved ones die, the family holds on to God's promise of a home.
As you read: Notice how the family remembers God's promise while living elsewhere.
Talk or reflect What hope does this family pass to the next generation?
Try this Write a hope you'd like to pass on.
Where do you see trust growing despite mistakes? Which family habits bring care, and which cause harm?
Next, this family becomes a people enslaved in Egypt. God begins to lead them out.
Ready to continue? Begin with the next section. Go at your own pace.
You are here Deliverance from Egypt and the wilderness journey
Next Israel Before It Had Kings
Where we are Jacob's family has settled in Egypt. A later king sees them as a threat and forces them into slavery.
The big question How will Israel learn to live freely with God and each other? Leaving Egypt is only the beginning.
People Moses; Aaron; Miriam; Pharaoh; Joshua; Caleb
Places Egypt; the sea crossing; Sinai; the wilderness; the plains of Moab
A little help as you begin

God rescues Israel before giving them laws. Exodus tells of rescue and God's covenant, or shared promises. Leviticus explores worship. Numbers follows life in the wilderness. Deuteronomy prepares the next generation. Ask what each law meant for ancient Israel before applying it today. Notice care for people in need. When Israel struggles, consider how you respond to uncertainty, too.

Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. 1 Corinthians 5:7 connects Jesus with Passover. John 3:14-15 uses the lifted serpent. Hebrews 8-10 explains priests, the sanctuary, and sacrifices in relation to Jesus. Read each connection in its own passage.
As you read: God's rescue and presence, care for neighbors, and trust during hard times.
Pause here After Readings 025, 033, and 043, ask how worship shapes daily life.
What would you like to understand as you begin?
In this reading A new king fears Israel's growing numbers and enslaves them. God hears their cries and calls Moses.
As you read: Notice the courage of people whose names receive little public attention.
Talk or reflect Who shows courage when others are afraid?
Try this Pray for courage to care for someone with less power.
In this reading Moses confronts Pharaoh, who keeps refusing God's command. The plagues show the limits of Egypt's power.
As you read: Follow Pharaoh's changing words alongside his continuing refusal.
Talk or reflect What is missing from Pharaoh's promises?
Try this Think of one way to follow a promise with action.
Passover, Exodus, and the Red Sea
In this reading Passover marks Israel's rescue. At the sea, God opens a way when the people feel trapped.
As you read: Notice the movement from fear to rescue, remembrance, and song.
Talk or reflect How can remembering help when people are afraid?
Try this Write down one kindness you don't want to forget.
Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. First Corinthians 5:7 uses Passover imagery for Christ. John 19:36 also invokes Scripture about unbroken bones in its account of Jesus' death.
In this reading Israel leaves Egypt and enters the wilderness. Hunger, thirst, conflict, and shared work test their trust.
As you read: Watch how provision and shared responsibility sustain the journey.
Talk or reflect How do people share needs and responsibilities in the wilderness?
Try this Ask for today's help and share a burden if you can.

Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. John 6:30-35 recalls manna while Jesus speaks of the true bread from heaven. Compare the gift in the wilderness with what Jesus claims to give.
Sinai, the Law, and the Covenant
In this reading At Sinai, God gives the rescued people guidance for life with him and care for their neighbors.
As you read: God rescues Israel before giving these commands. They are not a way to earn rescue.
Talk or reflect Which command shows care for a neighbor?
Try this Try one small act of fairness or honesty.

Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. Matthew 5:17-20 explains Jesus' relationship to the Law and the Prophets. Read his teaching before deciding that Sinai has either no relevance or identical direct application today.
In this reading God gives plans for the tabernacle, a place of worship among his people. Many skills will help build it.
As you read: Notice how the tabernacle's spaces teach respect for God and ways to approach him.
Talk or reflect What helps people approach God with both joy and respect?
Try this Take a quiet moment before your next prayer.

Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. Hebrews 8:1-6 discusses the sanctuary in relation to Jesus' priestly ministry. Its own comparisons provide firmer guidance than assigning a hidden meaning to every measurement.
The Golden Calf and Covenant Renewal
In this reading While Moses is away, Israel makes a golden calf. Moses pleads for the people, and God offers renewed mercy.
As you read: Notice how impatience turns visible objects into substitutes for trust.
Talk or reflect What might help Israel trust while waiting for Moses?
Try this Bring an uncertainty to God and give yourself time to listen.
Connection to Jesus A shared Christian theme. Moses' intercession raises questions about mercy and representation. Hebrews 3:1-6 compares Moses and Jesus while also distinguishing their roles.
In this reading The people build the tabernacle with willing gifts and skilled work. God's glory fills it.
As you read: Notice the partnership of generosity, craftsmanship, and obedience.
Talk or reflect How do ordinary skills help the whole community?
Try this Offer a skill where it could help someone.
In this reading Leviticus opens with different offerings for worship, thanks, wrongdoing, and restored relationships with God.
As you read: Notice how the offerings differ. Each has its own purpose.
Talk or reflect What do the different offerings express?
Try this Consider a practical way to give thanks or make amends.

Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. Hebrews 10:1-14 contrasts repeated offerings with Christ's self-offering. Study both the original sacrificial setting and Hebrews' later argument.
In this reading Priests begin their service. A serious failure soon shows how much care their role requires.
As you read: Notice that spiritual leadership carries accountability as well as privilege.
Talk or reflect Why does leadership call for care and honesty?
Try this Pray for people who carry responsibility, including yourself.
Ceremonial and Physical Cleanliness and Purification
In this reading Israel receives rules for ritual purity and bodily life. Illness is not treated as proof of personal wrongdoing.
As you read: Ritual uncleanness is not the same as personal wrongdoing or lesser worth.
Talk or reflect How can people care for illness without adding shame?
Try this Choose words that respect someone living with illness or weakness.
Atonement and the Sacredness of Blood
In this reading The Day of Atonement brings cleansing for people and the sanctuary. Rules about blood underline the value of life.
As you read: Notice the difference between everyday offerings and this annual ceremony.
Talk or reflect What does this ceremony show about making things right with God?
Try this Thank God for mercy and consider any harm that needs care.
Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. Hebrews 9:6-14 uses the Day of Atonement setting to explain Christ's work. The connection is developed in the biblical text itself.
In this reading God's guidance reaches into family, work, fairness, and care for neighbors. Worship belongs with everyday life.
As you read: Look for protection of the poor, the stranger, and those easily exploited.
Talk or reflect Where do these laws protect everyday relationships?
Try this Choose fairness when it would be easy to take advantage.
Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. Jesus cites the command to love one's neighbor in Matthew 22:39. Let the wider setting in Leviticus deepen the command's practical meaning.
In this reading Rules guide priests and offerings. Limits on altar service do not make a physical condition a sin; Leviticus 21:22 preserves access to sacred food.
As you read: Notice the different rules for purity, altar service, and conduct. Priests with limits on their service still receive care.
Talk or reflect How can a community take worship seriously and honor every person?
Try this Bring care and respect to one shared responsibility.
In this reading Israel's calendar makes room for worship, rest, and release. Sabbath and Jubilee affect work, land, debts, and relationships.
As you read: Notice how sacred time affects land, labor, debt, and relationships.
Talk or reflect What do these rhythms of rest make possible?
Try this Plan a small space for rest, with care for others too.

Connection to Jesus A shared Christian theme. Luke 4:16-21 announces good news and release through Isaiah's language. Jubilee can enrich reflection on release, but it is not a simple blueprint for every modern policy.
In this reading Leviticus closes with warnings, promises, and guidance about vows. Faithfulness involves daily life together, not only ceremonies.
As you read: Read warnings alongside the possibility of confession and remembered covenant.
Talk or reflect What helps a promise last?
Try this Take one manageable step toward keeping a commitment.
In this reading Israel dedicates the sanctuary and prepares the Levites. The first-month Passover comes before the census in the second month.
As you read: Numbers 7 recalls the dedication; Numbers 9:1 dates Passover before the census in Reading 035. The Levites' preparation has no separate date.
Talk or reflect How do gifts and service help people take part?
Try this Thank someone whose contribution helps others join in.
In this reading Israel is counted and organized for travel. Guidance about service, making amends, and blessing shapes life in the camp.
As you read: Numbers 1:1 dates the census after the Passover in Reading 034. The nearby laws do not date every instruction.
Talk or reflect What helps shared life stay both orderly and kind?
Try this Choose one dependable way to help.
In this reading God's cloud guides Israel away from Sinai. As the journey begins, complaints and challenges test the community.
As you read: Numbers 10:11 dates the departure after the dedication, Passover, and census. Numbers 9:15-23 describes the cloud's ongoing guidance.
Talk or reflect What helps people stay honest and hopeful under pressure?
Try this Recall something true and helpful when worries grow.

Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. First Corinthians 10:1-13 uses wilderness episodes to warn Christians against presumption. Paul's point is accountable faithfulness, not superiority over Israel.
In this reading Scouts return from Canaan with different views of the same land. Fear spreads, and the people refuse to enter.
As you read: Distinguish acknowledging difficulty from declaring God's promise impossible.
Talk or reflect How do the scouts' different views affect the people?
Try this Listen to someone who can name both the difficulty and the hope.
In this reading Rebellion challenges Israel's leaders. The story asks how people should handle authority, questions, and responsibility before God.
As you read: Notice how leaders and the community answer for their choices.
Talk or reflect How can people raise concerns about leadership with care?
Try this Ask for humility in both leading and asking questions.
In this reading The journey brings grief, conflict, and unexpected help. Israel continues learning to trust God through change.
As you read: Notice the bronze serpent episode within the larger pattern of complaint and mercy.
Talk or reflect What makes asking for help easier?
Try this Bring a need to God, just as it is.

Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. John 3:14-15 compares the lifted serpent with the lifting up of the Son of Man. Follow the comparison Jesus makes rather than extending it without limits.
In this reading Balak hires Balaam to curse Israel, but blessing follows instead. Balaam's words and motives raise questions about spiritual leadership.
As you read: Compare Balaam's words with his motives and limits.
Talk or reflect How can people look beyond impressive religious words?
Try this Ask for wisdom to notice character as well as words.
Judgment, the Second Census, and Joshua
In this reading A new census prepares the next generation. Women ask for a fair hearing, and Joshua receives responsibility after Moses.
As you read: Notice the daughters of Zelophehad asking for a just hearing.
Talk or reflect Whose concern needs a fair hearing?
Try this Make room to listen to someone who has been overlooked.
Offerings, Vows, and the Eastern Tribes
In this reading Offerings, promises, and plans for settlement shape shared life. The eastern tribes must also care about the wider community.
As you read: Notice the responsibilities attached to receiving a place to live.
Talk or reflect How do one group's choices affect others?
Try this Keep a commitment that helps someone else move forward.
In this reading Israel remembers the wilderness journey and prepares for life in the land. Psalm 90 reflects on time and human limits.
As you read: Read Moses' prayer alongside the record of travel, loss, and preparation.
Talk or reflect What does Moses' prayer suggest about using our time?
Try this Make time for one thing that matters.
In this reading Moses helps the next generation remember the past. Earlier failures can become lessons for what comes next.
As you read: Notice how retelling the past can teach without trapping people in it.
Talk or reflect How can a hard memory become a useful lesson?
Try this Write one lesson from Israel's journey.
The Covenant and the Call to Love God
In this reading Moses calls Israel to love God wholeheartedly and teach the next generation through ordinary daily life.
As you read: Watch for remembering, loving, hearing, and practicing rather than information alone.
Talk or reflect What do everyday habits teach the next generation?
Try this Add a small reminder of God's care to your day.
Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. Jesus joins Deuteronomy 6:5 with Leviticus 19:18 in Mark 12:28-34. Love for God and neighbor belongs together.
In this reading Guidance for worship, leaders, giving, and justice connects love for God with care for neighbors.
As you read: Notice the limits placed on rulers and the protections offered to vulnerable people.
Talk or reflect What helps leaders use their power well?
Try this Welcome a boundary that protects other people.
In this reading Laws address courts, families, work, and strangers. God's guidance reaches places where people can easily be hurt.
As you read: Look for principles of fairness while respecting the ancient legal setting.
Talk or reflect Who might be affected by a decision that seems convenient?
Try this Consider the person with the least power before deciding.
In this reading Moses calls Israel to choose life. Alongside warnings, there is hope of returning to God after failure.
As you read: Notice how love, listening, and obedience belong together.
Talk or reflect Which choices help life grow?
Try this Try one caring action you could repeat tomorrow.
In this reading Moses blesses the tribes and dies before entering the land. Psalm 91 adds words of refuge during this change.
As you read: Promises of protection invite trust, not reckless tests of God.
Talk or reflect How can trust make room for grief and care?
Try this Entrust an unfinished task to God and those who follow.
Connection to Jesus The New Testament explains the link. In Matthew 4:5-7, Psalm 91 is quoted during Jesus' temptation. Jesus refuses to turn a promise of care into a reason to test God.
Which wilderness struggle feels familiar? What could help you remember God's care?
Moses dies before the crossing into Canaan. Joshua will lead the next stage of the journey.
Ready to continue? Begin with the next section. Go at your own pace.
You are here Settlement in Canaan and the period of the judges
Where we are Moses has prepared Israel to enter the land. Joshua now leads them toward their new home.
The big question Will Israel keep trusting God? Again and again, people turn away, suffer, receive help, and turn away once more.
People Joshua; Deborah; Gideon; Jephthah; Samson; Ruth; Naomi; Boaz
Places The Jordan; Jericho; Israel's tribal territories; Bethlehem
A little help as you begin

Joshua tells of entering the land and choosing to follow God. This plan places Judges 17-21 early, partly because Phinehas is still present. The exact years are unknown. Later judges bring rescue but also fail. Ruth belongs to this period, though her dates are uncertain, and leads toward David's family. Remember: describing violence or a harmful vow does not approve of it.

A little help as you begin

Acts follows the growing church. The letters help real communities with real needs; some dates and placements are debated. Read each letter as a connected message. Revelation uses visions, symbols, warnings, and hope to call people to Jesus. The journey ends with new creation, returning to themes from Genesis. Take time to notice how your reading has grown.

Meet some of the people and places along the way. Use the references as starting points when you'd like to read more.
Adam and Eve The first people in the creation story. Their choices introduce human worth, responsibility, and broken trust.
Noah God preserves him and his family through the flood and gives a promise for the future.
Job A man whose suffering challenges the idea that pain always results from personal wrongdoing.
Abraham and Sarah God promises them family, land, and a blessing that will reach others.
Isaac and Rebekah Their family carries God's promise forward, though their choices also bring conflict.
Jacob Also called Israel. His descendants become Israel's tribes.
Joseph Sold into Egypt, he later helps his family survive a famine.
Moses God calls him to confront Pharaoh, lead Israel, teach God's guidance, and prepare the next generation.
Aaron and Miriam Moses' brother and sister. Both help lead Israel.
Joshua The leader after Moses who brings Israel into Canaan and calls them to remain faithful.
Deborah A prophet and judge who helps guide Barak and Israel toward rescue.
Ruth and Naomi Their story of loss and loyal care leads to new belonging and David's family line.
Samuel A prophet and judge who leads during Israel's move toward having kings.
Saul Israel's first king. His story shows the harm caused by fear, jealousy, and refusing to listen.
David A king linked with Jerusalem and God's promise. He also causes serious harm and must face his wrongdoing.
Nathan A prophet who brings God's promise to David and later confronts his wrongdoing.
Solomon David's son and the next king, known for wisdom and the temple, but also for divided loyalty.
Elijah and Elisha Prophets who challenge rulers and bring help to ordinary households.
Isaiah A prophet who brings Judah and other nations warnings, comfort, and hope of renewal.
Jeremiah A prophet during Judah's crisis and Jerusalem's fall. He also shares God's promise of a new covenant.
Ezekiel A prophet living among the exiles. His visions speak of judgment, renewal, and God's presence.
Daniel A faithful servant under foreign rulers who receives visions of kingdoms and future hope.
Ezra and Nehemiah Leaders who help people learn, rebuild, and renew shared life after exile.
Esther A Jewish queen who risks her position and life to help protect her people.
John the Baptist A prophet who prepares the way for Jesus and calls people to turn toward God.
Mary Jesus' mother. She is a different person from Mary Magdalene and the other Marys in the Gospels.
Peter A leading disciple who fails, receives a fresh start, and helps others follow Jesus.
Paul Also called Saul. Once a persecutor, he is called to share Jesus, especially with people who are not Jewish.
Barnabas A generous encourager who helps welcome Paul and works alongside him.
Priscilla and Aquila A couple who welcome, teach, and support others in the church.
Timothy Paul's coworker, who teaches and cares for churches.
John Several people share this name, including the Baptist and Zebedee's son. Take care with who is meant and questions about who wrote the books linked to John.
Eden The garden in the opening human story. Its exact location is not known.
Canaan The land promised to Israel's ancestors and later settled by Israel. Its ancient boundaries do not match one modern country.
Haran A place in northern Mesopotamia important in Abraham's and Jacob's family stories.
Egypt Joseph rises to power here. Israel settles, becomes enslaved, and later leaves under Moses.
Sinai The mountain where Israel receives God's covenant guidance. Its location today is debated.
The Jordan Israel crosses this river into Canaan. Later, John baptizes people here.
Jericho A city near the Jordan, important in Joshua's story and Jesus' ministry.
Bethlehem Associated with Ruth's family, David, and Jesus' birth.
Hebron A place in the ancestors' stories and the center of David's early rule in Judah.
Jerusalem Judah's royal and temple center. Jesus' final ministry, death, and resurrection take place here.
Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, and the Gospels
Samaria The northern kingdom's later capital. The name also describes a region in the Gospels and Acts.
Assyria and Nineveh Assyria conquers northern Israel. Nineveh is a major Assyrian city addressed by prophets.
Babylon The city and empire that take Judah into exile. Revelation also uses Babylon as a symbol.
Persia and Susa Persian rulers allow return and rebuilding. Susa is the court setting of Esther's story.
Galilee The northern region where much of Jesus' public ministry takes place, including around the lake.
Nazareth The Galilean town where Jesus grows up.
Antioch Syrian Antioch helps send out missionaries. It is different from Pisidian Antioch in Acts 13.
Ephesus A city in Roman Asia where Paul works and where a church later receives letters.
Macedonia and Greece Areas Paul visits, including Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, and Corinth.
Rome The empire's capital. Acts ends with Paul sharing Jesus here.
Patmos The island where John receives the visions described in Revelation.

Allegory A story or picture whose details point to another meaning. In Galatians 4:21-31, Paul uses Abraham's family to explain two covenants. Follow the writer's links rather than looking for a hidden meaning in every detail.

Apostle Someone sent with a message or task. The New Testament often means those Jesus sends, including the Twelve and Paul. It can also mean messengers sent by churches; see Galatians 1:1 and 2 Corinthians 8:23.

Atonement God's work to overcome sin and restore life with him. In Israel's worship, it includes cleansing people and sacred places; see Leviticus 16:16. Through Christ's life, death, and resurrection, God offers forgiveness, healing, and freedom from destructive powers. His work renews hearts and lives, not only our standing before him.
Blessing A gift of God's goodness that helps life grow and equips us to care for others. It may bring strength through difficulty, not an easy life.
Canon The books received as Scripture. This plan follows the Protestant Bible's 66 books.
Chronology The order of events in time. Some biblical dates and sequences remain uncertain.
Covenant A relationship shaped by promises and commitments. God's covenants show his faithfulness and care. Each also has its own setting and responsibilities.
Diaspora People living away from their ancestral homeland. In the Bible, this often means Jewish communities in other nations.
Disciple A learner who follows a teacher. Here, it usually means someone learning Jesus' ways and putting them into practice. Other teachers also have disciples; see Luke 5:33.
Exile Being forced from home. The Assyrian and Babylonian exiles are separate events. Both bring great loss and become settings for God's promises of renewal.
Exodus God's rescue of Israel from slavery in Egypt. It also names the book that tells this story and the beginning of Israel's new life together.
Faith Trust in God that leads us to rely on him and follow his guidance. It grows as we receive his truth and care.
Gentile Someone who is not Jewish. Acts and the letters show God's welcome reaching every people through Christ.
Gospel The good news of Jesus: God's love, victory over sin and death, and offer of restored life. The word also names the four accounts of Jesus' life.
Grace God's freely given kindness and help. He welcomes us before we earn anything and helps us grow in love.

Holiness Belonging to God and reflecting his goodness. God's character is pure and good. People, places, objects, and days can be set apart for his service. For people, holiness includes changed hearts, honest choices, and loving service. It does not make us superior to others.
Idol An object, image, or substitute given the trust that belongs to God. Idols can shape life around fear, selfishness, or false hopes.
Israel The name given to Jacob, his descendants, or the northern kingdom after the nation divides. The passage helps you tell which is meant.
Judah Jacob's son, the tribe descended from him, or the southern kingdom after the division. Jerusalem is that kingdom's center.

Justification Being set right with God through Christ. God welcomes those who trust Christ; his Spirit then renews their lives. Renewal grows from grace rather than earning it. The word can also mean recognizing someone as right: in Luke 7:29, people acknowledge God's goodness, not change him.
Kingdom of God God's rule of truth, love, and freedom, shown in Jesus. It grows in willing hearts and will be fully seen when God renews creation.
Lament An honest prayer or poem of grief, distress, or protest brought to God. It makes room for pain without rushing an answer or recovery.

Law Instruction, a rule, or a principle at work. It may mean the Torah, one command, or Israel's civil and worship rules. Romans 8:2 also uses it for the powers of sin and death, and of the Spirit's life. Read each use in context. God's moral guidance serves truth, love, and healthy relationships.
Levite A member of Levi's tribe who serves Israel's worship and community. Some Levites are priests; others have different roles.
Messiah The anointed one, whom Christians identify as Jesus. He reveals the Father, overcomes evil, and restores people to life with God.
Oracle A message from a prophet. Ask who first heard it and what its warning, promise, or invitation meant for them.
Parable A story or comparison that helps people see truth and examine their hearts. Look for its main teaching before seeking meaning in every detail.
Passover Israel's remembrance of rescue from Egypt. The New Testament connects it with Jesus' loving rescue from sin and death.
Pentecost The Jewish festival when the Holy Spirit comes in Acts 2. The Spirit helps the disciples share Jesus across languages and communities.
Priest Someone appointed to lead worship and represent people before God. Hebrews presents Jesus as our high priest, bringing us close to God and helping restore our lives.
Prophet A messenger of God's truth. Prophets name harmful choices, call people back, and offer hope. Their work is more than predicting the future.
Providence God's faithful care in creation and history. He works for good while honoring freedom. Trusting him does not mean knowing why every painful thing happens.
Redemption Rescue from bondage into freedom and life. Christ frees us from sin's destructive power through costly love. Some passages use the word for family duties or property rights.

Remnant Those who remain, often after disaster or exile. It may also mean a faithful community through whom God preserves hope. Surviving does not make someone morally better. Romans 11:5 emphasizes God's grace.
Repentance A change of heart and direction in response to God's goodness. It means facing sin's harm, receiving help, and turning toward a better way.

Resurrection God raising the dead to life. Jesus' resurrection gives hope beyond death. Scripture also speaks of resurrection to life and to judgment; see John 5:28-29 and Acts 24:15. Death does not have the final word.

Righteousness What is right and good in character, relationships, and actions. God's goodness includes truth, justice, mercy, and repair. Through trust in Christ and his Spirit's help, it grows within us and becomes honest, fair, loving action. It does not earn God's love.
Sabbath The seventh-day rest rooted in creation. It invites time with God and others, trust in his care, and remembrance of freedom and covenant faithfulness.
Sanctuary A place of God's presence and worship, especially the tabernacle or temple. It pictures his desire to live with his people and cleanse them from sin.
Sin Distrust, selfishness, and rebellion that separate us from God and harm ourselves and others. It affects our hearts and actions; without healing, it destroys life.
Tabernacle Israel's movable place of worship in the wilderness. It reminds the people that God is with them.
Temple The sanctuary in Jerusalem, built under Solomon and later rebuilt. The New Testament also uses this picture for Jesus and people in whom God's Spirit lives.
Torah A Hebrew word for instruction, especially the Bible's first five books. They tell Israel's beginnings and teach life with God.
Typology Seeing an earlier person, event, or practice as a pattern fulfilled more fully later, especially in Christ. Notice whether the Bible makes the link or a reader suggests it.
Wisdom Learning to live well with God's truth and love. It joins understanding, humility, and good choices that care for life and relationships.
Zion A name for part of Jerusalem, later used for the city and God's home among his people. Poems and prophecies use it to picture hope and renewal.
